Governments should ban single-use plastic products, because the environmental cost of convenience has become too high. Items like bags, straws, and cutlery are used for minutes but persist for centuries. They clog rivers, kill marine animals, and break down into microplastics that now appear in drinking water and human bodies.

Voluntary measures have not worked. Consumers are told to recycle, yet only a small fraction of plastic is ever recycled, and much of it is shipped abroad or dumped. A legal ban changes the default and forces industry to invest in alternatives.

Critics argue that bans hurt businesses and low-income households. These concerns deserve attention, but countries such as Kenya and several EU states have shown that transitions are manageable, especially with phase-in periods and support for small firms. Reusable and compostable options often become cheaper once they are produced at scale.

A ban on the most avoidable items, paired with incentives for innovation, is a reasonable and effective step. Convenience should not outweigh the health of the planet we all depend on.

There isn't one reason; it's a mix of practical needs and personal taste, and the mix differs a lot from owner to owner.

The original reason is function. A lift raises the body or suspension, which gives the truck more ground clearance so it can pass over rocks, ruts, and deep snow without scraping the underbody. It also makes room for bigger tires, which add more clearance and traction, and it improves approach and departure angles on steep terrain. People who actually go off-road, whether for hunting, trail riding, or ranch work, have good reason to do it. Competition adds to that: mud bogging, rock crawling, and desert racing all reward clearance and big tires, and many street trucks are built in the image of those rigs.

For many owners, though, looks matter more than capability. A lifted truck sits tall and wide on large wheels, and that aggressive stance makes a stock truck look timid by comparison. Truck building is also a hobby and a social scene. Clubs, meetups, and online forums give owners a way to swap ideas and parts, and a customized truck is a visible way to show personality, skill, and commitment. In some regions, a big lifted truck also signals toughness or belonging to a particular culture, and styles spread quickly when friends and neighbors adopt them.

There's a smaller comfort factor too. Sitting higher gives some drivers a better view over traffic and a feeling of security, although the extra height also creates bigger blind spots directly in front of the vehicle.

Lifts do have costs. They raise the center of gravity, which hurts handling and can increase rollover risk. They usually reduce fuel economy, put extra stress on suspension, steering, and driveline parts, and make the truck harder to climb into, park, and stop. Some states regulate maximum lift or bumper and headlight heights, and insurers may charge more for modified vehicles.

So some people lift their trucks because they truly need the capability, but many do it for the look, the hobby, and the identity that comes with it.

Mobile gaming video is one of the fastest-growing forms of online content, yet its perceptual quality has received far less attention than that of natural videos. Gaming content differs in important ways, with synthetic scenes, rapid motion, sharp graphical elements, and on-screen overlays, and it is often streamed or recorded on mobile devices under limited bandwidth. To study how these factors affect perceived quality, we constructed a new database of mobile gaming videos spanning a variety of games, compression levels, and resolutions, and conducted a large-scale subjective study to collect human opinion scores. We then benchmarked a broad set of existing objective video quality models on the database and found that many general-purpose methods perform poorly on gaming content, which motivates models designed specifically for it. The database and our findings aim to support future work on quality-aware streaming, encoding, and evaluation of mobile games.

The proverb "All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy" is a warning that someone who does nothing but work will become boring, tired and eventually less effective. It has been in English for centuries, with versions appearing in collections of proverbs as early as the 1600s.

**The idea behind it**

Play and rest are not the opposite of productivity. They are part of what makes it possible. A person who works constantly gets worn down. Concentration slips, creativity dries up, and stress piles up. Time spent on hobbies, friends and relaxation refreshes the mind, so the work that gets done afterward is usually better.

**Why "dull"?**

In this saying, "dull" works in two senses. Jack becomes dull in the sense of being uninteresting, with nothing to talk about except work. He is also dull in the sense of a blunt blade, a mind that has lost its sharpness. Both meanings suggest that constant effort without variety wears a person down.

**What research suggests**

Modern psychology supports the proverb. Studies on burnout show that people who rarely take breaks have lower motivation and more mistakes. Rest allows the brain to consolidate memories and make new connections, which is why good ideas often arrive in the shower or on a walk. Play also supports mental health, social bonds and problem-solving.

**A cultural echo**

The phrase is famously used in Stephen King's novel *The Shining* and Stanley Kubrick's film version, where Jack Torrance types the line over and over on page after page. It becomes a chilling symbol of isolation and obsession, which is the very thing the proverb warns about.

**Takeaway**

Balance is the point. Hard work matters, but a life without enjoyment is poorer and less effective. Make time to rest and play, and you will usually work better too.

Solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity through the photovoltaic effect. Most panels are built from silicon solar cells, which are wafers of silicon treated to create an electric field.

**Inside the cell**

Silicon is a semiconductor. To make a solar cell, manufacturers dope two layers differently. The top layer is infused with phosphorus, which adds extra electrons and makes it n-type. The bottom layer is doped with boron, which creates electron vacancies called holes and makes it p-type. Where the two layers meet, a p-n junction forms, creating a built-in electric field.

**Generating current**

When a photon with enough energy strikes the silicon, it knocks an electron loose from its atom, leaving behind a hole. This creates an electron-hole pair. The electric field at the junction pushes electrons toward the n-type side and holes toward the p-type side, separating the charges before they can recombine.

Metal contacts on the front and back of the cell collect these electrons. When an external circuit connects the contacts, the electrons flow through it as direct current, powering devices along the way before returning to the other side of the cell.

**From cell to system**

A single cell produces only about 0.5 volts, so dozens are wired in series within a panel. Panels are then connected in arrays. Because homes use alternating current, an inverter converts the DC output to AC. Anti-reflective coatings and textured surfaces help the cell absorb more light.

Typical panels convert roughly 18 to 23 percent of the sunlight that hits them into electricity.

In cold-weather climates, winter brings a mix of outdoor recreation, seasonal traditions, and practical routines.

**Outdoor sports and recreation.** Skiing, snowboarding, ice skating, and sledding are among the most popular activities. Many people also enjoy snowshoeing, cross-country skiing, and ice hockey, whether in organized leagues or on frozen ponds. Children build snowmen and have snowball fights.

**Ice fishing.** In places with thick lake ice, such as Minnesota, Canada, and parts of Scandinavia, people drill holes in the ice and fish from heated shelters.

**Seasonal traditions.** Winter holidays such as Christmas, Hanukkah, and Lunar New Year bring gatherings, decorations, and shared meals. Winter festivals, ice sculpture contests, and outdoor markets are common in many regions.

**Indoor activities.** Cold days often mean cooking hearty meals, baking, reading, watching movies, or playing board games.

**Practical tasks.** Shoveling snow, clearing driveways, and preparing homes and cars for freezing temperatures are routine parts of winter life.

The first judge who sentenced Elias Marrow to life in prison had been dead for a hundred and ninety years by the time Elias finished counting the bricks in his cell for the eleventh time.

He had not meant to be sentenced at all. He had meant to be forgotten. But in 1823, a magistrate in a damp northern town had hanged him for theft, and he had come back from the rope with a cough and an unpleasant headache. They tried again. Then they tried drowning. Eventually a clerk, a tidy man with ink on his sleeves, suggested the obvious: if the man could not be killed, he could at least be kept.

"Life," the judge had said, with more irony than he knew. "Let the sentence be served in full."

So Elias served it. At first he counted days, like everyone does. Then years. Then he gave up on numbers and started noticing the prison itself, how it changed around him. Candles became gas lamps. Gas lamps became bulbs. The guards' coats changed color. Their language drifted, and he learned the new words the way a man learns a river's moods.

Over time the prisoners learned something about him too. They called him the Old Man, though he looked about forty. New arrivals asked him the same questions: how long, how do you stand it, what's it like?

"It's like waiting for a train," he'd say, "except you've lost the timetable and the station keeps being rebuilt."

In the second century of his sentence, a young warden named Priya Ramanathan started visiting his cell with a clipboard and a stubborn expression. She was writing a report. She read the old records, compared signatures, and finally sat down across from him.

"The court that sentenced you doesn't exist," she said. "The country has changed its laws four times. Technically, there's no legal basis for you to be here."

Elias laughed, a dry sound he had not made in decades. "That's very kind. But I've been here so long that I wouldn't know where to go."

She came back the next week with a map. And the week after that, with a coat.

On the morning they opened the gate, there was fog, and the road beyond looked unfinished. The other prisoners lined the windows. He had expected to feel like a man escaping. Instead he felt like a man changing jobs.

"What will you do?" Priya asked.

Elias looked at the horizon, then at his hands, which had never aged and had never been free.

"Something slow," he said. "I have the time."

He stepped over the line where the wall's shadow ended. It was only a few inches of stone, but it took him a very long moment to cross.

Taking part in a school or university exchange programme is, in my opinion, a very good idea. First of all, it gives students the chance to experience a different culture directly. Reading about another country in a textbook is not the same as living there, trying the food, and seeing how people really spend their days. This kind of experience can make us more open-minded and less afraid of differences.

Exchange programmes also help students improve their language skills. When you have to order lunch or ask for directions in another language every day, you learn much faster than in a classroom. In addition, studying abroad builds independence. Students must solve problems on their own, from managing money to making new friends.

Of course, there are some disadvantages. Exchanges can be expensive, and some students may feel homesick or struggle with a new school system. However, I believe these difficulties help people grow stronger.

In conclusion, the benefits of exchange programmes, such as cultural understanding, language learning and personal growth, clearly outweigh the risks. I think every student who has the opportunity should try it.

Mermaids are mythical, so there is no real answer, but we can reason about it using biology. The short version is that mermaids would most likely lay eggs. The longer version depends on how you define a mermaid.

**The classic design**

The traditional mermaid has a human upper body and a fish tail. If you take that literally, the animal combines mammalian features with fish features, and the reproductive system is the big question. Mammals give live birth and nurse their young, while most fish reproduce by laying eggs or spawning. Which group a mermaid belongs to would determine the answer.

**Case for eggs**

The tail is the strongest clue. In most bony fish, females release eggs into the water, where they are fertilized externally. If mermaids evolved from fish, or share a deep ancestry with them, egg-laying is the default. It is also the easiest strategy for a fully aquatic creature, since eggs can be deposited in sheltered spots and the female does not need to carry the young while swimming.

There is also a practical point about the body plan. A streamlined tail built for swimming leaves little room for a long pregnancy. Carrying a large, human-sized baby inside a fishlike lower body would be physically awkward and risky.

**Case for live birth**

Mermaids with human features are usually pictured breathing air or at least surfacing, and as having hair, warm blood and breasts. Those traits point toward mammals, as with dolphins, whales and manatees. Marine mammals are proof that a fully aquatic animal can give birth to live young, nurse them with milk and care for them for years. If mermaids behave like cetaceans, they would be live-bearing.

**A middle path**

Nature offers hybrid strategies. Sharks and rays, for example, include species that lay eggs, species that give live birth, and species that hold eggs inside the body until they hatch. Platypuses and echidnas are mammals that lay eggs. So a mermaid could be a strange mix of traits without breaking the rules of biology.

**My conclusion**

Taking the fish tail seriously, I would say mermaids lay eggs. The evolutionary logic is simple: the tail suggests fish ancestry, and fish ancestry means external reproduction. The mammal-like upper body might be explained as convergent evolution, the way dolphins evolved fish-like shapes without being fish. But if you insist on a creature with human characteristics, live birth becomes more believable, with mermaids more like a human-sized cetacean.

Eggs are the more biologically likely answer for the classic design, and live birth is the more likely answer for the human-like version. It is one more reminder that mermaids are a mix of two very different animal groups, and reproduction is exactly where that mix runs into trouble.

Because light only looks like it travels in straight lines when it interacts with large objects and detectors. In quantum terms, light doesn't follow one path. It explores all possible paths, and each path carries a phase. For most situations, paths that stray from the straight line have phases that vary rapidly and cancel each other out. Only paths near the straight line add up constructively, so the beam appears straight. This is the idea behind Feynman's path integral formulation.

With a double slit, the opening is so small, comparable to the wavelength, that the cancellation fails. Many more paths survive, and they add up in a pattern that produces the bright and dark fringes. A wide opening restores straight-line behavior, and the beam spreads far less. Straight-line propagation is simply the large-scale limit of wave behavior.

# The Flat Earth Society

The Flat Earth Society is an organization that promotes the belief that the Earth is a flat disc rather than a sphere. It is the best-known group associated with modern flat-earth thinking, though the idea itself is far older than the society.

## Origins

The society traces back to Samuel Birley Rowbotham, an English writer who in the mid-1800s argued, based on experiments he performed along a canal called the Bedford Level, that the Earth had no curvature. His ideas were later developed by followers such as Lady Elizabeth Blount, who founded the Universal Zetetic Society in 1893. The modern Flat Earth Society was founded in 1956 by Samuel Shenton in England. After Shenton died in 1971, the group was led by Charles K. Johnson in California, who ran it for decades until a fire destroyed its records and he died in 2001. The society was relaunched as a website and online community in the 2000s.

## What members believe

Most versions of the model describe the Earth as a disc with the North Pole at the center and Antarctica forming an ice wall around the outer edge. The sun and moon are said to be relatively small and to circle above the disc. Members typically claim that photographs from space are faked or distorted, that governments and space agencies are involved in a cover-up, and that observations like ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon have alternative explanations such as perspective or atmospheric effects.

## Scientific consensus

The spherical shape of the Earth is supported by an enormous body of evidence. Examples include the way different constellations are visible at different latitudes, the curved shadow the Earth casts on the moon during lunar eclipses, time zones, circumnavigation by air and sea, satellite observations, and direct measurements by surveyors going back to Eratosthenes, who estimated Earth's circumference more than two thousand years ago. No credible scientific institution disputes this.

## Modern profile

The society gained more attention in the 2010s as flat-earth content spread widely on social media and video platforms. Conferences have been held, and some celebrities and athletes have publicly expressed sympathy for the idea. Researchers who study conspiracy beliefs often note that flat-earth views appeal to people who distrust institutions, and that the movement is as much about skepticism of authority as about geography.

Some observers have long wondered whether the society is entirely serious. Regardless, its members insist they are sincere, and the organization continues to operate today.

**Abstract**

The acoustic radiation force and torque exerted on a small particle by a sound field are commonly interpreted through energy and pressure considerations. Here we show that, for particles much smaller than the wavelength, these quantities can instead serve as direct measures of the canonical momentum and spin angular momentum densities of the field. Using a dipole approximation of the particle's scattering response, we derive expressions that separate the force into components proportional to the curl-free canonical momentum density and the curl-spin density, and relate the torque to the spin density of the acoustic field. We apply the formalism to representative fields, including standing waves, evanescent waves, and vortex beams, and show that it accounts for transverse forces and spin-dependent effects not captured by conventional descriptions. The results provide a unified physical picture of acoustic momentum and spin, and suggest experimental approaches to measuring them using small probe particles.

My eyes were the first thing the nurses noticed. Not blue, brown, or green, but black from edge to edge, with no line between iris and pupil. My mother told me she had cried for an hour, and then she had stopped, because I had stared up at her like I was memorizing her face.

In my town, eyes were destiny. Gold eyes meant strength. Green eyes meant you could talk to plants. Blue eyes meant water, and the Pellman twins, both blue, had spent a summer making the whole pond rise on command. At eighteen, your power woke, and everyone came to the party to watch the color flare in your irises like a struck match.

So everyone knew what mine would be, and nobody knew, and that was the problem.

"Maybe nothing," my cousin Dara said once, not unkindly. "Maybe black means blank."

I turned eighteen on a Thursday in October. The whole street showed up anyway, standing around our yard with paper cups, trying not to stare at me too hard. My mother held my hand. At midnight, I closed my eyes and waited.

Nothing happened.

No flare. No heat. No light. People shifted. Somebody coughed. Dara looked at her shoes.

I opened my eyes and the porch light went out.

Then the streetlamp. Then the one at the end of the road, and the neighbor's windows, and the stars, I think, though I couldn't say for sure. The dark came in like water, quiet and total, and the paper cups slipped from people's fingers. Someone screamed. A child began to cry.

I was terrified. I wanted it to stop, and so, it did. The lights flickered back, one by one, and I understood what I was holding. It wasn't the power to hurt. It was the power to take away light, and to give it back.

My mother pulled me into her arms. "That's it?" she whispered, laughing. "That's all?"

It wasn't all, of course. In the months that followed, I learned that the dark had a texture, that I could fold it around a person like a coat, and that it could hide a girl who was being chased through the woods. Dara showed me how. Black eyes didn't mean blank. They meant I was the only one who could see what the others couldn't.

I started carrying a flashlight, just in case. It's strange to be afraid of the dark when you are the dark. But I like to think that's the part that keeps me kind.

Good morning. My name is Ruth Aldana, and I am here to present Form 9-C, Application to Take One Life, in accordance with Article Four of the Allotment Act.

The Subject is Thomas Brandt, aged forty-one. Section Two requires a description of the harm. On the night of March third, Mr. Brandt drove through a red light at sixty-one miles per hour. My husband, Samuel, died at the scene. Mr. Brandt served fourteen months. I have attached the court records, the toxicology report, and eleven letters from his neighbors, each describing him as a good man. The Committee should know that I read every one.

Section Three asks whether lesser remedies were exhausted. They were. I pursued civil damages, which Mr. Brandt paid in full, and I received a written apology, which is also attached. I did not reply to it.

Section Four concerns necessity. My prepared statement runs to four pages, but it may be summarized in one sentence: the law was satisfied, and justice was not.

The Chair raised one hand. "Thank you, Ms. Aldana. Before you continue, please read Section Eleven aloud."

I turned the page. "Describe your anticipated circumstances one year following approval."

I had rehearsed every other answer in the mirror for three years. I had skipped this one, assuming it was a formality.

The room was silent. I could picture the act in precise detail, and nothing at all after it: no kitchen, no morning, no chair where Samuel used to sit.

"I would like to withdraw the application," I said, "under Article Seven."

"Withdrawal is permitted. Your allotment remains with you." The Chair stamped the form WITHDRAWN without looking up. "For the record, most applicants prepare for the question of the Subject. Few prepare for the question of themselves."

I gathered my papers and the eleven letters, and walked out into the morning.

I do not agree that young people today have less respect for older generations. I think they show respect in different ways.

In the past, young people always used formal words and stood up for older people. Today, many young people are more relax and they talk to teachers and parents like friends. Some older people think this is rude, but I think it is only a different style. For example, my friends and I call our teacher by her first name, but we still listen to her and we thank her for help.

Also, young people today help older people in many ways. I teach my grandmother to use her smartphone, and she is very happy when she can see photos of her family. Many students also do volunteer work at nursing homes or help old neighbors with shopping. These things show real respect.

Of course, some young people are not polite. They are noisy on the bus, or they look at their phones when older people talk to them. But I think this happened in every generation, not only now.

In conclusion, I think young people respect older people just as much as before. The way is different, but the feeling is the same. It is important that both groups listen to each other.

Cavemen did get cavities, but far fewer than most modern people, and the reasons come down mostly to diet. Their teeth also did wear down and fall out in many cases, just for different reasons than ours.

**Why cavities were rare**

Tooth decay is mainly caused by bacteria that feed on sugar and refined carbohydrates, producing acid that dissolves enamel. Prehistoric hunter-gatherers ate very little of either. Their diets consisted of meat, fish, nuts, roots, wild vegetables and seasonal fruit. Honey was occasionally available, but there was no refined sugar, no soda and no sticky processed snacks that cling to teeth all day.

Archaeological evidence supports this. Studies of skeletons from before the development of farming show low rates of cavities. Cavities became much more common after agriculture spread roughly 10,000 years ago, when people began eating large amounts of grain, such as wheat, barley and maize. Starchy foods break down into sugars in the mouth, giving decay-causing bacteria a steady supply of fuel.

**They did clean their teeth, in a way**

Early humans did not use toothbrushes, but they were not completely neglectful. Researchers have found toothpick grooves on fossil teeth from Neanderthals and earlier hominins, which shows that people picked food out from between their teeth. They probably also chewed on twigs, bones or fibrous plants, which would have cleaned the surface a little.

In addition, a diet of tough, raw or lightly cooked food required a great deal of chewing. This vigorous action stimulated saliva flow, and saliva neutralizes acids and washes away bacteria. Fibrous foods like roots and raw vegetables also scrub the teeth as you eat them.

**Other dental problems**

Prehistoric people did suffer from tooth problems. The biggest was wear. Grit from stone grinding tools, dust, sand and tough food ground down enamel, sometimes exposing the pulp inside and leading to infection. Abscesses are well documented in ancient remains. Gum disease also existed, and tartar, the hardened plaque that builds up on teeth, appears frequently on ancient teeth. Scientists actually use that calcified plaque today to learn what ancient people ate, and even to study their microbiomes.

Injuries added to the problem, since teeth were sometimes used as tools to hold hides, soften materials or grip objects. Without dentists, an infected tooth could be dangerous or even deadly.

**Did their teeth fall out?**

Some did lose teeth, especially older individuals. Because many people died young, however, widespread tooth loss in old age was less visible than it is today. Those who survived into their forties or fifties often had worn teeth, and some had lost several.

**Our situation today**

Interestingly, modern humans have more cavities despite brushing, flossing and professional care. This is because our consumption of sugar is so high that it overwhelms our protection. A typical caveman likely had better teeth than many people who skip dental visits, simply because his food was not constantly feeding the bacteria in his mouth.

Another point is that oral bacteria changed after farming. Analysis of ancient dental plaque shows that the mouth microbiome became less diverse as diets shifted to farming and later to processed food, and that shift is linked to higher levels of disease-causing bacteria.

**Summary**

Cavemen avoided most decay because they ate little sugar, chewed hard fibrous foods, and produced lots of saliva. They cleaned their teeth with picks and twigs, but their real advantage was diet. They still suffered from wear, abscesses and gum disease, and without any medical care these problems could be serious. Brushing is valuable for us because our diet is so different from theirs.

**Abstract**

Speaker verification with short utterances remains challenging because limited speech duration yields unreliable i-vector estimates and degrades recognition accuracy. This paper proposes a transformation method that uses conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) to map i-vectors extracted from short utterances toward the distribution of those obtained from long utterances. The generator is conditioned on the short-utterance i-vector and trained adversarially against a discriminator, while an additional regression objective preserves speaker-discriminative information. The transformed i-vectors are subsequently scored using a standard probabilistic linear discriminant analysis back-end. Experiments on the NIST SRE corpora under multiple utterance durations demonstrate consistent reductions in equal error rate relative to the baseline system and to conventional compensation techniques. The results indicate that conditional adversarial learning is an effective approach for improving verification performance under short-duration conditions.

# From 100 Rejections to One Big Lesson: Entrepreneur Finds Success in Saying "No"

An entrepreneur whose startup dream began with a string of refusals says the experience turned out to be the best thing that ever happened to his career.

Jia Jiang set out to build a company but found that fear of being turned down was holding him back. So he did something unusual. For 100 days, he deliberately sought out rejection, making strange and often awkward requests of strangers, and recorded the results in a project he called "100 Days of Rejection."

The challenge pushed Jiang far outside his comfort zone. What began as a personal experiment in overcoming discomfort became a quest that reshaped how he thought about risk, work, and ambition. By the end, what had started as a stunt had turned into an unexpected success.

"It's not rejection itself that hurts us the most," Jiang has said of the lessons he took from the project. "It's the fear of it."

That idea sits at the center of his story. According to Jiang, many people avoid asking for what they want, whether it is a job, an investment, or a simple favor, because they imagine how painful a "no" would feel. In practice, he found, the response is often far less harsh than expected. Sometimes the answer is even "yes."

The project drew a wide audience, and Jiang's account of it struck a chord with people who recognized their own hesitation in his. His story has since been held up as an example for aspiring founders and anyone facing a daunting goal.

For Jiang, the takeaway is simple. Rejection is a part of any ambitious effort, and learning to face it is a skill that can be practiced. Those who wait until the fear disappears, he says, may be waiting forever.

Tunka-Rex is a radio antenna array for the detection of air showers induced by high-energy cosmic rays. It is built as an extension of the Tunka-133 array of non-imaging air-Cherenkov detectors in the Tunka Valley in Siberia, close to Lake Baikal, and records the radio emission of air showers in the frequency band of 30–80 MHz. Because radio waves are emitted mainly by the electromagnetic component of the shower, are only weakly attenuated in the atmosphere, and can be measured with an almost 100% duty cycle, the radio technique is an attractive and relatively inexpensive complement to established detection methods. Its measurements are triggered by Tunka-133, which independently determines the energy and the depth of shower maximum from the Cherenkov light of the same events. This makes it possible to cross-calibrate the two techniques and to determine how precisely radio measurements can reconstruct these key shower parameters. Particular attention is paid to the energy range above 10¹⁷ eV, where the transition from galactic to extragalactic cosmic rays is expected. In this contribution we present the layout and hardware of the array, including the antennas, the analog signal chain, and the data acquisition system, which shares the infrastructure of Tunka-133. We describe the calibration procedures and give an overview of the status of the first stage of the experiment and of the first measurements.
